items.prompt: What does the padlock in the address bar tell you?
choices: The company behind the site is trustworthy
The page has been scanned for malware
The connection to this domain is encrypted
The site never collects personal data
items.explanation: The padlock is about the connection and the domain, not the character of the site's owner.

items.prompt: What is HTTPS?
choices: HTTP running inside an encrypted TLS connection
A faster HTTP that compresses every page
A separate protocol that replaced the web
HTTP that only works on mobile networks
items.explanation: HTTPS is ordinary HTTP carried over TLS, so the requests are the same but the wire is protected.

items.prompt: In the envelope story, what does the seal protect?
choices: The honesty of the shop at the door
The spelling of the name above the shop
The city office's stamp from being copied
The letter while it travels the road
items.explanation: The seal is the encryption: it only covers the trip, not who receives the letter.

items.prompt: In the story, what did the city office check before stamping the card?
choices: That the shop bakes good bread
That the person controls the name on the door
That the owner is a decent person
That no similar shop name exists
items.explanation: The stamp is domain validation: control of a name, nothing about quality or intent.

items.prompt: Can a phishing site show a valid padlock?
choices: No, browsers refuse certificates to phishing sites once reported
Yes, if its owner controls a domain and gets a certificate
Only if the page copies the real site pixel for pixel
Only if the site is hosted in a different country
items.explanation: Anyone can register a domain and request a certificate for it, lookalike names included.

items.prompt: Which of these is NOT something the padlock promises?
choices: The data is hidden from eavesdroppers
The data cannot be edited in transit
The certificate matches the domain shown
The domain belongs to the brand you expect
items.explanation: Brand ownership of a domain is outside what a certificate states.

items.prompt: After you see a padlock, what is still your job to check?
choices: The exact spelling of the domain name
Whether the padlock icon looks green or grey
How quickly the page loads on a slow phone
How many images the page shows at once
items.explanation: The match is strict about the string, but only you can tell paypa1 from paypal.

items.prompt: A stranger on cafe Wi-Fi records your traffic to a padlocked site. What do they get?
choices: Your password in plain text
The full page text without the images
Scrambled bytes they cannot read
Your form fields but not your cookies
items.explanation: TLS makes the contents unreadable to anyone on the path.

items.prompt: A user follows an emailed link to bank-secure-update.net, sees a valid padlock, and types a password. What is the most accurate conclusion?
choices: The password reaches the bank because the link looked official
The password is exposed because phishing sites cannot use TLS
The password is safe because a CA reviewed the site's owner
The password travels privately to whoever controls that domain
items.explanation: Encryption protected the trip to bank-secure-update.net, which may be run by an attacker. The padlock never said whose domain it was.
items.reference:
Two promises, two gaps
encrypted in transit: yes
domain matches the certificate: yes
domain is the brand you meant: not covered
site operator is honest: not covered
Why: the padlock covers the road and the exact name on the door, and nothing about who is behind the door.
items.learnMore:
What the padlock covers

Encryption keeps the contents private on the way, and the certificate ties the connection to one exact domain. Everything about who runs that domain and why is left to the reader and to other defences.

Common mistake

Reading a padlock as a safety rating for the site. It is a statement about the connection.
items.reflection: Think of a sealed package from a courier. What would the seal not tell you about the sender? Where else do you rely on a guarantee that covers only part of what you assume?

items.prompt: Which pairing correctly separates what the padlock proves from what remains the reader's job?
choices: Operator honesty on the server, versus whether the data is encrypted
Encrypted to this domain, versus whether this is the right domain
Brand identity of the owner, versus whether the domain is spelled correctly
Server safety against attacks, versus whether the connection is private
items.explanation: The padlock covers the connection and the domain match; deciding that the domain is the one you meant stays with the reader.

choices: HTTPS only encrypts the images on the page and never the login form itself
HTTPS certificates are refused to login pages by most CAs
HTTPS secures your traffic, not other people's lookalike domains
HTTPS turns off the padlock for visitors on mobile browsers
items.explanation: Attackers can host their own HTTPS lookalike. Your certificate protects your visitors' traffic to you, not other people's domains.

choices: Someone on the network path reading or editing pages in transit
Attackers registering lookalike domains for the brand
Bugs in the server's own code leaking user data
Users clicking links in convincing phishing emails
items.explanation: TLS addresses the in-transit risk. Lookalikes, server bugs, and deceived users are separate problems.

items.prompt: A certificate binds a public key to what?
choices: A domain name
A visitor's password
A page's visible content
A server's connection speed
items.explanation: A certificate says that this public key belongs with this domain name.

items.prompt: Who signs a site's certificate?
choices: The visitor's own browser
The site's hosting provider
A certificate authority
A randomly chosen visitor
items.explanation: A CA's signature is the proof that the key and the name belong together.

items.prompt: What is a root certificate?
choices: The first certificate a site ever received
A CA certificate that browsers already trust
A certificate stored only on one server
The oldest certificate on a visitor's device
items.explanation: Roots ship inside browsers and operating systems and anchor every chain.

items.prompt: Why do CAs use intermediate certificates?
choices: To make pages load faster for every visitor on slow links
To store each website's private key safely for its owner
To remove the need for any root certificate at all
So the root key can stay locked away and rarely used
items.explanation: Intermediates sign day-to-day certificates, which limits exposure of the root's key.

items.prompt: Which order lists a chain from the site upward?
choices: Root, leaf, intermediate
Intermediate, root, leaf
Leaf, intermediate, root
Leaf, root, intermediate
items.explanation: Each certificate is signed by the next one up, ending at a trusted root.

items.prompt: What must the browser already have to verify a new site?
choices: The root certificates it trusts
A list of every website's certificate
A copy of each site's private key
A saved password for each CA
items.explanation: The browser trusts a few roots in advance and works out the rest from signatures.

items.prompt: Which three things does a certificate carry?
choices: A private key, a password, and a signature
A public key, a username, and a cookie
A private key, a domain name, and an address
A public key, a domain name, and a signature
items.explanation: The private key never appears in a certificate.

items.prompt: What happens if a signature in the chain is invalid?
choices: The page loads with a padlock anyway
The browser shows a warning page
The browser quietly switches to HTTP
The browser asks the site for a new root
items.explanation: A broken link means the chain no longer proves anything, so the browser warns.

items.prompt: A leaf certificate is signed by an intermediate, which is signed by a root missing from the browser's trust list. What happens?
choices: It is trusted, since every individual link in the chain has a valid signature
It is not trusted, since the chain ends at an unrecognized root
It is trusted, since the leaf names the right domain
It is trusted, since the intermediate has a known name
items.explanation: Valid signatures only matter if the chain ends at a root the browser already trusts.
items.reference:
A chain, drawn upward
leaf: names one domain
intermediate: signs leaves
root: already trusted by the browser
one broken signature: warning page
Why: trust flows down from a pre-trusted root through signatures, so the browser needs no prior knowledge of the site.
items.learnMore:
Why chains instead of a list of sites

A browser cannot know every site, so it trusts a small set of roots and follows signatures. Intermediates exist so a root key does not sign every certificate itself.

Common mistake

Thinking the browser stores a list of trusted websites. It stores a list of trusted signers.
items.reflection: Passports, notarized documents, and diplomas all rely on someone you trust vouching for someone you do not know. Where in daily life do you follow such a chain without noticing?

items.prompt: Why can a browser trust a site it has never visited before?
choices: Many other users have visited the same domain before
Its server sent a password the browser accepted
Its owner appears in a global register of brands
Its certificate chains to a root already trusted
items.explanation: Trust travels along the signature chain from a pre-trusted root, not from familiarity.

items.prompt: What does the signature on a leaf certificate protect?
choices: That the key-to-domain pairing was not altered
That the domain owner is a registered company
That the private key stays secret
That the site is free of flaws
items.explanation: A signature detects alteration of the signed contents. It says nothing about the company or the site's bugs.

items.prompt: Which compromise damages the whole trust system the most?
choices: Theft of one website's private key
Theft of one visitor's browser cache
Theft of a root CA's signing key
Expiry of one website's certificate
items.explanation: Anyone holding a trusted root's key could mint certificates for any domain, which is why roots stay locked away.

items.prompt: Which two checks sit at the core of a padlock?
choices: The logo matches the brand and the page loads fast
The brand is real and the owner is honest
The server is nearby and cookies are fresh
Name matches and signatures reach a trusted root
items.explanation: Name match plus a valid signature chain is what the verifier answers.

items.prompt: The name check compares the certificate's domain to what?
choices: The page title shown on the tab
The domain in the address bar
The server's average response time
The username the visitor typed in
items.explanation: The certificate must name exactly the domain you are visiting.

items.prompt: Does a valid chain prove the business behind the site is legitimate?
choices: Yes, the CA phoned the business
Yes, but only for large companies
No, only that signatures and the name line up
Yes, if the certificate is not expired
items.explanation: Legitimacy is a fact about the world that no signature encodes.

items.prompt: What does an expired certificate cause?
choices: A warning, even if the chain is otherwise valid
Nothing, since expiry is never checked
A padlock with a slower connection
A silent switch to a different CA
items.explanation: Expiry is a separate check, and failing it triggers a warning.

items.prompt: Which problem would the verifier NOT catch?
choices: A lookalike domain with its own valid certificate
A certificate edited after it was signed by the CA
A certificate issued for a completely different domain
A chain that ends at a root nobody recognizes
items.explanation: A lookalike passes every check for its own name.

items.prompt: A certificate for example.org is shown at example.com. What happens?
choices: A normal padlock
A request for the visitor's password
A name mismatch warning
A silent redirect to example.org
items.explanation: The certificate names a different domain than the address bar.

items.prompt: Does a phishing site on its own domain pass the verifier?
choices: No, verifiers are built to recognize phishing pages
Yes, it passes both checks for its own domain
No, phishing domains cannot be given certificates
Only if it copies the original certificate bytes
items.explanation: The verifier only checks the domain it was handed.

items.prompt: Who has to notice that paypa1 is not paypal?
choices: The certificate authority at issue time
The root certificate in the chain
The signature algorithm in use
The reader of the address bar, or a separate filter
items.explanation: Telling lookalikes apart is outside what the chain can do.

items.prompt: A lookalike domain presents a valid chain and a matching name, so the padlock appears. Why is the verifier not wrong?
choices: It was fooled by a forged signature on the leaf
It skipped the name check for this domain
It answers a narrower question than the visitor is asking
It trusts any root that appears in a chain
items.explanation: The verifier decides whether this name has a valid certificate, not whether you meant this name.
items.reference:
What each check answers
name match: is this the domain in the bar?
signatures: did a trusted root vouch for it?
expiry: is it still in date?
brand check: not performed
Why: every check asks whether the certificate is valid for the name, never whether the name is the one you meant.
items.learnMore:
Narrow checks, honestly answered

The verifier gives exact yes or no answers to name, signature, and date questions. A lookalike passes because those are the only questions on the list.

Common mistake

Reading a passing verifier as an endorsement. It is a set of narrow technical answers.
items.reflection: A bouncer checks that your ticket is real, not that you are a good guest. Where else does a perfectly good check answer a narrower question than the one you care about?

items.prompt: A certificate for shop.example.com is presented while visiting shop.example.org, with an otherwise valid chain. What is the outcome?
choices: It fails because the certificate names a different domain
It passes because the chain is valid up to a trusted root
It passes because both names share the word shop
It fails because an intermediate cannot sign two names
items.explanation: Name match is its own check, and a perfect signature chain cannot rescue a wrong name.

items.prompt: A team adds an expiry check to the verifier. How much does that help against lookalike domains?
choices: A lot, since lookalikes nearly always run on very old certificates
Some, since expired lookalikes are detected earlier
A lot, since expiry reveals the real brand owner
None, since a fresh lookalike certificate is not expired
items.explanation: Expiry says the certificate is still in date. A new lookalike certificate is as current as any.

items.prompt: Which pair of facts can be checked offline from the certificate data alone?
choices: Brand legitimacy and the signature validity
The name match and the signature validity
Operator intent and the name match
Operator honesty and the root's age
items.explanation: Names and signatures are in the data. Brand legitimacy and intent are facts about the world.

items.prompt: What does a domain-validated certificate prove?
choices: The requester is a registered business
The requester controls the domain
The requester is based in your country
The requester has a clean record
items.explanation: DV checks control of a name and nothing else.

items.prompt: How fast is domain validation usually?
choices: Weeks, with paper forms
Days, after a phone interview
Months, after a legal review
Minutes, fully automated
items.explanation: Automation is the whole point of DV.

items.prompt: Does DV involve a human reviewing the request?
choices: No, it is an automated challenge
Yes, an officer studies every name
Yes, but only for short names
Yes, but only on weekdays
items.explanation: No person looks at the request, which is why it scales.

items.prompt: How can a requester prove control of a domain?
choices: Send a scanned photo of a valid business license
Attend an in-person interview at a CA office
Publish a value the CA provides on the domain
Share a recent company bank statement
items.explanation: The CA hands out a challenge and checks that it appears under the domain.

items.prompt: What does extended validation (EV) add?
choices: A faster handshake
A stronger encryption algorithm
A longer lifetime for the key
Checks on the organization behind the domain
items.explanation: EV adds identity checks about the organization.

items.prompt: Why was domain validation made cheap and automatic?
choices: Because CAs wanted to serve fewer customers overall
So HTTPS could be adopted by the whole web
Because browsers had decided that no checks were needed
Because phishing sites had asked for it
items.explanation: Cheap, automatic certificates made universal HTTPS practical.

items.prompt: Does a DV certificate say who runs the site?
choices: Yes, it lists the owner's address
Yes, it lists the owner's tax number
No, only that someone controls the domain
Yes, it lists the owner's bank
items.explanation: DV contains no organization identity.

items.prompt: Can someone get a DV certificate for a lookalike domain they registered?
choices: Yes, if they control that lookalike domain
No, the CA always blocks any similar-looking names
Only if the real brand gives its approval
Only if they pay extra for extended validation
items.explanation: The challenge only tests control, so any controlled domain qualifies.

items.prompt: A CA issued a certificate for a PayPal lookalike in minutes. How should this be described?
choices: Domain validation working as designed; it never judged names
A CA failure, since lookalikes should have been blocked
A browser bug, since the padlock should have been hidden
A protocol flaw, since TLS itself should reject similar-looking names
items.explanation: The DV contract is control of the domain. Judging names was never part of it.
items.reference:
DV versus EV
DV: proves control of the domain
DV: automatic, minutes, no human
EV: also checks the organization
browsers: show both the same way now
Why: a certificate is as informative as the check behind it, and the common check is only about domain control.
items.learnMore:
Why validation stays light

Automatic checks let nearly every site use HTTPS. Anything requiring human judgment would turn certificates back into a slow, costly service.

Common mistake

Expecting the CA to know your intent. It only checked who controls the name.
items.reflection: A library card proves you live in town, not that you will return the books. When does a cheap, quick check beat a thorough one, and who then carries the risk it leaves?

items.prompt: Why can't DV simply add a review of whether the name resembles a brand?
choices: Certificates have no field that is able to hold a brand name
Brands refuse to hand their names to any CA for checking
Human-style judgment cannot run in minutes at web scale
Browsers would ignore any extra review result beyond the signature
items.explanation: Cheap, automatic issuance and human-style judgment pull in opposite directions.

EV certificates are refused by most browsers

items.explanation: The extra checks still happen, but users cannot see the difference.

A review that compared the name to known brands
A payment that unlocked a trust rating

items.explanation: They proved control of their own domain, and nothing more was asked.

items.prompt: When does the TLS handshake happen?
choices: After the page has fully loaded
Only when the visitor logs in
Before any page data moves
Once a day per browser
items.explanation: The handshake sets up the keys that protect everything that follows.

items.prompt: What does ClientHello contain?
choices: Supported versions and cipher suites
The visitor's password and chosen username
The page the visitor wants to read first
The server's private key and certificate
items.explanation: The browser opens by listing what it can do.

items.prompt: What is a cipher suite?
choices: A list of banned websites
A folder of saved certificates
A password for the server
The bundle of algorithms agreed for the connection
items.explanation: Both sides pick one set of algorithms to use together.

items.prompt: Why negotiate a cipher suite instead of fixing one?
choices: It makes certificates cheaper for the CA to issue and renew
Weak algorithms can be retired without breaking everyone
It lets every visitor choose their own style of padlock
It removes the need for any handshake before page data
items.explanation: Negotiation lets TLS evolve while older and newer software still connect.

items.prompt: The server signs its key-exchange value with which key?
choices: The visitor's public key
The private key matching its certificate
The root CA's private key
A random password
items.explanation: Only the real certificate holder can produce that signature.

items.prompt: What protects the page data after the handshake?
choices: The certificate's public key used on every packet
A plain text password sent by the browser
The CA's signature attached to every packet
Symmetric encryption using the shared secret
items.explanation: Symmetric encryption is fast enough for bulk data.

items.prompt: How many round trips does a TLS 1.3 handshake need?
choices: 1 round trip
2 round trips
3 round trips
0 round trips
items.explanation: TLS 1.3 completes the handshake in a single round trip.

items.prompt: With an 80 ms round trip, how long does a TLS 1.2 handshake take in this unit's demo?
choices: 80 ms
240 ms
160 ms
320 ms
items.explanation: Two round trips of 80 ms each give 160 ms.

items.prompt: Why can't an attacker on the wire substitute their own key-exchange value?
choices: The value is encrypted with the browser's own private key file
The browser ignores any value arriving over the network
The certificate already contains the server's secret key
They cannot sign it with the key matching the certificate
items.explanation: The signature ties the value to the certificate holder, and an attacker lacks the private key.
items.reference:
Handshake, step by step
1. hello: versions and suites offered
2. certificate: checked against a trusted root
3. key exchange: signed by the cert key
4. both sides derive the same secret
Why: the certificate proves who is on the other end, and key exchange makes a secret that never travels.
items.learnMore:
What the handshake buys

Before the first byte of the page moves, both sides agree on algorithms, verify identity with the certificate, and compute a shared secret. Fewer round trips mean the page starts sooner.

items.prompt: Implement `matchesName(certName, host)`. A plain name matches only an equal host. A name starting with `*.` matches a host whose first label is non-empty and whose remaining labels equal the rest of the pattern. Ignore letter case.

*.example.com does not match example.com
*.example.com does not match a.b.example.com
names compare without regard to letter case
Why: a wildcard stands for exactly one label, so the rest of the host must equal the rest of the pattern.
